```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 96,
  dev = "jpeg",
  dev.args = list(quality = 90),
  out.width = "100%"
)
imgt_dir <- path.expand(Sys.getenv("SIRUP_IMGT_DIR"))
has_trees <- nzchar(imgt_dir) && dir.exists(imgt_dir)
```

Most studies have more than one tissue section. You may have several
sections from one donor, bulk AIRR-seq of the same tissue, or blood from
other time points. If
you call clones on all of them together, one clone ID means the same lineage
in every sample. You can then ask where a clone was seen.

One SIRUP object can hold all of this:

* `spatial` can be a named list of Seurat objects, one per section.
* The receptor table holds the rows from every section and every bulk sample.
  A `sample` column tells SIRUP which section each row belongs to.
* Rows whose `sample` does not name a section stay in the table as nonspatial
  rows. SIRUP does not put them on a tissue, but clone calling, trees, and
  your own summaries can use them.

This vignette follows Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. The MG thymus data come
from a patient who had a thymectomy. Besides the two Visium sections, there is
bulk BCR-seq of the thymus, and of blood taken at the thymectomy and 12 months
later. We ask which eGC clones also appear in the blood.

## Set up

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r load}
extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")

spatial <- list(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds")),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
)

read_bcrs <- function(file, sample, compartment) {
  airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, file)) %>%
    mutate(sample = sample, compartment = compartment)
}

sections <- bind_rows(
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice1"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2", "thymus_slice2")
) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  )

bulk <- bind_rows(
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_1", "bulk_thymus"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_2", "bulk_thymus"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_1", "blood_month0"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_2", "blood_month0"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_1", "blood_month12"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_2", "blood_month12")
)

bcrs <- bind_rows(sections, bulk) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))

count(bcrs, compartment, sample)
```

`read_bcrs()` reads one AIRR file and adds two columns: `sample` and
`compartment`. After the barcodes come out of the section IDs, the code makes
each `sequence_id` unique and tree-safe. It puts the sample name in front,
because IDs repeat between files, and it replaces the comma with `_`, because
dowser renames tree tips that contain a comma. The spatial rows get a `sample` that
matches the names of the `spatial` list. The bulk and blood rows have their
own sample names and no barcode.

To keep the package small, the bulk files hold a subset of the bulk data: the
blood sequences of clones seen in a section, and up to 10 bulk thymus
sequences of each clone that reaches the blood.

## Create a multi-sample object

Give `createSIRUP()` the named list and the `sample` column:

```{r create}
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = spatial,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  sample = "sample",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)

sirup
spatialSamples(sirup)
```

Visium barcodes repeat between sections: `AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1` exists in both.
SIRUP matches each receptor to a spot by the pair of sample and barcode, so
the two sections never mix.

If the sections need different image settings, give named values:
`image_scale = c(mg_thymus_slice1 = "hires", mg_thymus_slice2 = "lowres")`.

## Get one sample

The accessors take a `sample` argument:

```{r accessors}
getSpatial(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1"))
nrow(getReceptors(sirup))
```

`filterSample()` returns a new SIRUP object with one section. It drops the
nonspatial rows:

```{r filter-sample}
slice1 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
slice1
```

`subsetSIRUP()` gives finer control. It can keep a set of spots, a set of
receptor rows, and, with `keep_nonspatial_receptors = TRUE`, the bulk rows.

To go the other way, `mergeSIRUP()` combines single-section objects into a
multi-sample object. It adds a sample column with the names you give:

```{r merge}
slice2 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice2")
merged <- mergeSIRUP(
  slice1, slice2,
  samples = c("mg_thymus_slice1", "mg_thymus_slice2"),
  sample_field = "sample"
)
merged
```

## Add polygons for each section

Give `addPolygons()` a named vector of polygon files, one per section:

```{r polygons}
sirup <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons_path = c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
))

getPolygons(sirup)
```

Both files number their eGCs from 1, so SIRUP adds the sample to each polygon
ID: `mg_thymus_slice1::1` and `mg_thymus_slice2::1` are different regions.

## Plot several sections

By default, a spatial plot of a multi-sample object returns a list with one
plot per section. Set `combine_sample_plots = TRUE` to get one combined
figure, or give `sample_id` to plot one section:

```{r plots, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, zoom = TRUE, combine_sample_plots = TRUE)
```

```{r plot-one}
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1",
  title = "AICDA, section 1"
)
```

## Call clones across all samples

Call clones on the whole receptor table, so that one clone ID covers the
sections, the bulk thymus, and the blood:

```{r clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup)$clone_id)
```

## Where was each clone seen?

Each row has a `compartment`. For each clone, count its sequences in each
compartment, and record the eGCs that hold it:

```{r presence}
clones <- getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  summarise(
    in_section = any(compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2")),
    n_egc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)),
    egcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", "),
    n_bulk_thymus = sum(compartment == "bulk_thymus"),
    n_blood_month0 = sum(compartment == "blood_month0"),
    n_blood_month12 = sum(compartment == "blood_month12")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    in_egc = n_egc > 0,
    in_blood = n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12 > 0
  )

count(clones, in_egc, in_blood)
```

Most clones stay in the thymus. A few eGC clones also appear in the blood.
The paper calls these clones exported. Fisher's exact test compares the eGC
clones with the other clones of the sections:

```{r fisher}
section_clones <- filter(clones, in_section)
fisher.test(table(section_clones$in_egc, section_clones$in_blood))
```

Count, for each eGC, the clones it holds and the clones that reach the blood:

```{r per-egc}
getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  filter(!is.na(polygon_id)) %>%
  distinct(polygon_id, clone_id) %>%
  left_join(select(clones, clone_id, in_blood), by = "clone_id") %>%
  group_by(polygon_id) %>%
  summarise(n_clones = n(), n_exported = sum(in_blood)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_exported))
```

The example data hold a subset of the bulk data, and the clones come from
that subset. For the full analysis, see Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper.

## Clonal dominance in every section

Regional functions work on all sections at once. The dominance table has a
`sample` column and the full `polygon_id`:

```{r dominance}
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup, locus_val = "IGH")

dominance$dominance %>%
  group_by(polygon_id) %>%
  slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(sample, polygon_id, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion) %>%
  head()
```

Most plotting functions return a named list with one plot per section:

```{r region-receptors}
region_plots <- plotSpatialRegionReceptors(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  top_n = 8,
  point_size = 1.5,
  zoom = TRUE
)
names(region_plots)
region_plots$mg_thymus_slice1
```

`plotSpatialPolygonPies()` also works on all sections at once. Give
`sample_id` to draw the pies of one section next to its map:

```{r pies, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6}
pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  top_n = 5,
  sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1"
)
pies$page_1
```

## A tree with blood tips

A lineage tree can mix spatial and bulk sequences. Pick an exported eGC clone
with blood sequences from both time points:

```{r pick-clone}
exported <- clones %>%
  filter(in_egc, n_blood_month0 > 0, n_blood_month12 > 0) %>%
  mutate(n_total = n_egc + n_bulk_thymus + n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12) %>%
  filter(n_total <= 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12))
exported

tree_clone <- exported$clone_id[[1]]
tree_section <- sub("::.*$", "", exported$egcs[[1]])
tree_section
```

Make its germline with `dowser::createGermlines()`, then build its tree. As in
`vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP")`, the germline step needs
the IMGT references in the folder that `SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` names, and the tree
chunks run only when that folder exists. Keep `compartment` in `traits`, so
we can set the tip shapes by compartment:

```{r tree, eval = has_trees}
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id == tree_clone)
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  tree_sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  references = dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir),
  id = "sequence_id"
)
tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  id = "sequence_id",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "sample", "compartment", "polygon_id")
)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(tree_sirup)
trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
```

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` puts the spatial tips on their sections. Bulk
and blood tips appear in the tree only. Here `shape_by` sets one shape per
compartment and `color_by` colors the tips by tree cluster:

```{r tree-plot, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
trees <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = "auto", id = "sequence_id", k_range = 1:6)

pair <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  shape_by = "compartment",
  shape_values = c(
    thymus_slice1 = 21, thymus_slice2 = 21, bulk_thymus = 22,
    blood_month0 = 24, blood_month12 = 23
  ),
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black"
)

names(pair)
```

The list has one element per clone. When the tips of a clone fall in more
than one section, it has one element per clone and section instead, named
`<clone>::<sample>`, and each one pairs the full tree with the map of one
section. Each element also holds a `legend` for the tip shapes and colors.
Show the section that holds the eGC tips:

```{r tree-plot-show, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
key <- paste0(tree_clone, "::", tree_section)
if (!key %in% names(pair)) key <- tree_clone
section_pair <- pair[[key]]

cowplot::plot_grid(
  cowplot::plot_grid(section_pair$tree, section_pair$spatial_clone, rel_widths = c(1.3, 1)),
  section_pair$legend,
  ncol = 1,
  rel_heights = c(1, section_pair$legend_rel_height)
)
```

Circles are tips from a section, squares are bulk thymus, triangles are blood
at the thymectomy, and diamonds are blood 12 months later.

## Save the object

```{r save}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
readSIRUP(path)
```
